sentences.text: Every picture in the last act leaned on the risk model. So here is a comforting fact about it.
For every one of our two hundred providers, observed equals expected, exactly. Every meter is level.
Here is a second crowd, fitted the same way. Its two hundred meters are level too.
One of these two models is badly wrong. From here, you cannot tell which.
That is because the fit itself levels these meters. Episode 6 showed how: balancing is what fitting means.
A check that every model passes is no check at all. We need to cut the patients another way.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: trusting the risk model.
Forget the providers for a moment. Line up all 28,848 patients by the risk the model gives them, from lowest to highest.
Cut the line into ten equal groups, and give each group a meter of its own.
For the first crowd, the ten meters barely tilt. Observed over expected runs from 0.95 to 1.05.
Every one of those is within what luck allows. This model passes.
Now the second crowd. In its lowest-risk tenth, the model expected 136 readmissions. There were 339: two and a half times as many.
In the middle, the meters tilt the other way: more than a fifth fewer than expected.
Here is what went wrong. In this crowd, risk does not rise in a straight line with the first risk factor. It bends: patients at either extreme are at higher risk than a straight line allows.
The model was given a straight line, and did the best it could.
Give it the bend, as a squared term, and the ten meters settle: from 0.92 to 1.08.
Did the bend matter for the providers? It did. Between the two fits, 16 of the 200 change their flag.
And the fifth of providers with the most unusual case mix had ratios 16% too high. They were being blamed for the model's mistake.
There is a famous one-number summary of a risk model: the AUC. Take one patient who was readmitted and one who was not. The AUC is the chance that the model gave the first the higher risk.
For the wrong model, it is 0.74. For the corrected one, 0.76.
A tenth of the patients were off by a factor of two and a half, and the AUC barely noticed. It measures ranking, not whether the risks are right.
One more caution. In the first crowd, the AUC is 0.72 from the risk factors alone, and 0.74 once the model knows each patient's provider.
That gain says providers differ. It does not say the risk rule got any better.
A third cut: inside one provider. Our largest has 484 patients, and for them, in this experiment, risk climbs twice as steeply as the shared rule allows.
Its total balances, as it must: 143 observed, 143 expected.
But split its patients into a lower-risk half and a higher-risk half. 18 against 41. And 125 against 102.
One gamma cannot describe this provider. It is an average over the patients it happens to treat, and a direct rate built on it would mislead.
Software can catch some trouble before fitting: missing values, a risk factor that never varies, two that say nearly the same thing.
But every check today compared the model with data we have. None can see a risk factor that nobody recorded.
And more is not always better. Adjust for something a provider causes, such as a complication, and you adjust its performance away.
Let's gather it up.
Provider meters are level by construction. They prove nothing.
So take the same meter to new groups: tenths of risk, and halves within a provider.
And the AUC measures ranking, not fairness.
Throughout this series, each provider has had a number of its own, estimated on its own. Many analysts would do it differently, and pull the small providers toward the average.
Next time: fixed or random?
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
